title: Optimize technical deep dive — cache hit-rate + telemetry requirements
summary: Northstar Assist evaluated Redwood Optimize with a focus on prefix/KV cache hit-rate: what “hit” means for their workload (chat + long system prompts), how to normalize prompt prefixes to increase re-use, and what telemetry they need to trust the numbers (hit/miss/partial, hit-bytes, saved-prefill-ms, cacheable prompt ratio, plus attribution by route/model/version/region). Redwood shared the direction of cache telemetry v2 and discussed cardinality/sampling constraints (avoid request_id, hash prefix buckets, aggregate at route/model). Northstar’s main pain: they see cache hit-rate reported by their current stack but can’t correlate to latency savings due to partial-prefill and streaming retries. Call ended with a plan to share example dashboards/queries, run a 2-week pilot on a Dedicated pool, and provide Northstar sample guidance for prefix normalization (templates, tool-call ordering, and “stable prefix” rules).
topics: Workload characteristics (chat, long system prompts, tool calling, retries)
What counts as a cache hit vs partial hit vs miss
Prefix normalization and prompt template hygiene
Telemetry fields needed for trustworthy cache effectiveness
Dashboards: hit-rate, hit-bytes, saved-prefill-ms, cacheable prompt ratio
next_steps: Redwood (Renee) to share cache hit-rate dashboard screenshots + query examples (hit-rate, hit-bytes, saved_prefill_ms) by 2025-02-13.

Redwood + Northstar to schedule a 60-min pilot kickoff (Dedicated, us-east + eu-west) and define baseline measurements by 2025-02-18.
Northstar (Maya) to confirm acceptable data retention / PII constraints for telemetry and whether hashed prefix buckets are acceptable by 2025-02-18.

transcript:
Fireflies.ai — Transcript (auto-generated)

Meeting: Optimize technical deep dive — cache hit-rate + telemetry requirements
Date: 2025-02-11
Start time: 17:02 UTC
Duration: 53 minutes

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Renee Sullivan, Aditya Rao, Logan Wright, Omar El-Sayed
Northstar Assist: Jin Park, Alina Kovacs, Maya Thompson, Ben Ward

---

[00:00] Renee Sullivan: Cool. Alright, I think we’re good. Fireflies is recording. Thanks everyone for making time. Today we said we’d go deep on cache hit-rate—prefix / KV cache specifically—and what Optimize needs to generate the “increase hit-rate” recommendations.

[00:18] Ben Ward: Yep. Thanks Renee. We’re mostly trying to figure out like… is the hit-rate real, can we trust it, and then what can we do about it.

[00:27] Renee Sullivan: Makes sense. Quick intros, and then we can jump in. I’m Renee, I’m on the Solutions side, I work with product and platform teams on pilots.

[00:35] Aditya Rao: Aditya, product for Optimize.

[00:38] Logan Wright: Logan, I’m on telemetry/analytics. I own the cache telemetry spec internally.

[00:43] Omar El-Sayed: Omar, runtime. I’ve been living in the prefix cache for… too long.

[00:49] Jin Park: Jin, platform engineering at Northstar. I run the inference platform and routing.

[00:54] Alina Kovacs: Alina, ML engineer. I own prompt templates and evals, mostly.

[00:58] Maya Thompson: Maya, SRE. I’m the one that gets paged when latency goes weird.

[01:03] Renee Sullivan: Great. Ben?

[01:05] Ben Ward: Product. I’m accountable for the assistant feature, so I’ll ask annoying questions about user experience.

[01:10] Renee Sullivan: Perfect. So, maybe Jin, can you set context: what are you running today and what’s the caching pain?

[01:18] Jin Park: Sure. We have a mix. For some stuff we use OpenAI, but for the in-product assistant we run open models on our own GPUs. We’re currently on a vLLM-based stack, plus some homegrown routing. We tried enabling prefix caching and we do see like, 40 to 60% hit-rate reported, but the p95 time-to-first-token doesn’t move the way we’d expect. Sometimes it gets worse during spikes.

[01:43] Maya Thompson: And the dashboards we have are not great. It’s like one number, “hit-rate,” and we can’t break it down by route or model version without exploding Prometheus.

[01:53] Alina Kovacs: Also our prompts are messy. There’s a stable-ish system prompt, then tools, then we add dynamic stuff. I’m not sure what counts as “same prefix.”

[02:02] Renee Sullivan: Yep. That’s exactly the problems this sprint is trying to solve on our side too. Maybe Omar, could you give the 60-second on what we mean by prefix/KV cache in Redwood terms, and why hit-rate is slippery?

[02:14] Omar El-Sayed: Yeah. So, in our runtime we’re caching the KV states from the prefill stage—so the expensive “read prompt and build attention cache” part. If you can reuse that KV for the same prefix, you skip part of prefill next time.

[02:28] Omar El-Sayed: But “hit” can mean a few things. You can have a full hit, where the entire prefix is reused, or a partial hit where like the first N tokens match, then it diverges. Partial still saves compute, but not as much. Then there’s streaming retries, tool-call restarts, request cancellations—those can make metrics lie if you count events wrong.

[02:48] Ben Ward: What do you mean streaming retries?

[02:50] Omar El-Sayed: Like if the client disconnects and you retry the same request, or your gateway replays a request due to a timeout, it can look like a miss + hit combo depending on correlation.

[03:01] Logan Wright: Or you see “hits” but no latency savings, because the “hit” is only 10% of the prompt and the rest is still prefill. That’s why we’re pushing “hit-bytes” or “hit-tokens” and “saved_prefill_ms,” not just rate.

[03:15] Maya Thompson: That’s already more nuanced than what we have.

[03:18] Renee Sullivan: Okay, let’s anchor on your workload. Alina, what’s typical prompt shape? Like lengths and what changes.

[03:26] Alina Kovacs: For the assistant, we do a long system prompt—like 800 to 1,200 tokens. Then we add a tool schema. We use function calling. The tool definitions can be big, depends on the customer. Then conversation history, then user message. The system part is mostly identical per “mode,” but we do insert customer name, plan tier, sometimes a policy snippet based on region.

[03:52] Aditya Rao: That’s a classic “looks stable but isn’t” prefix. Even one token difference early breaks the exact prefix match unless you normalize.

[04:01] Jin Park: We also do routing by customer tier. So like enterprise goes to a bigger model and we do a smaller one for long tail. That splits the cache.

[04:09] Logan Wright: Cache fragmentation by route/model is huge. Optimize can recommend “pin model version for this route” if we see the same prompt prefix spread across multiple model versions or regions. But we need telemetry to prove it.

[04:23] Maya Thompson: Can you define what telemetry exactly? Like what fields. We’re very sensitive to cardinality.

[04:30] Logan Wright: Yeah. So the core metrics we think you need are:
- cache_outcome counts per request: hit, miss, partial
- hit_bytes or hit_tokens: how much of the prompt prefix was served from cache
- saved_prefill_ms: estimated prefill time avoided
- cacheable_prompt_ratio: fraction of prompts that are actually eligible for caching (not too short, not bypassed)

[04:52] Logan Wright: Then the minimal tags for breakouts are tenant (or account), route, model, model_version, region, and deployment_mode. But we cannot allow raw request_id or raw prompt_hash as a tag—those blow up.

[05:07] Jin Park: Tenant + route + model + version + region is already a lot.

[05:12] Logan Wright: Totally. The key is aggregation and sampling. You can do per-request structured events sampled at, say, 1% for debugging. But the counters/histograms that feed dashboards need strict tag budgets. We use hashed buckets for “prefix cluster” optionally, like 64 or 128 buckets, not unique hashes.

[05:29] Maya Thompson: So like a “prefix_bucket=17” kind of thing?

[05:32] Logan Wright: Exactly. Enough to identify “there are many distinct prefixes” vs “this is one stable prefix,” without letting you reconstruct prompts.

[05:41] Ben Ward: I’m going to ask: do we have to send prompts to you?

[05:44] Renee Sullivan: No. We don’t want your raw prompts. The goal is telemetry about cache behavior, not content. For Dedicated you can also keep telemetry in your VPC depending on setup, but for the Optimize recommendations we’d at least need the aggregate metrics.

[05:58] Jin Park: We are leaning Dedicated anyway. We probably can’t do fully hosted for this workload.

[06:04] Aditya Rao: That matches what we’ve seen. Optimize is available across Hosted and Dedicated, but the “deep” telemetry is easiest to roll out in Dedicated pilots because you control versions and routing.

[06:15] Alina Kovacs: Coming back to prefix normalization. What’s realistic guidance? Like, what would you tell me to do?

[06:23] Aditya Rao: A few patterns. First: keep the top of the prompt extremely stable. Don’t insert customer name in the first 50 tokens if you can help it—push dynamic fields later. Second: normalize tool definitions order and formatting—don’t generate JSON with non-deterministic key order. Third: separate “policy snippets” into a known set of templates and reference them rather than injecting custom text each time.

[06:49] Omar El-Sayed: Also be careful with whitespace and hidden tokens. We’ve seen “smart quotes” or slightly different markdown bullets break caching. It’s dumb but it matters.

[06:58] Alina Kovacs: Great… love that.

[07:01] Maya Thompson: So your recommendations would literally say “move dynamic fields later”?

[07:04] Aditya Rao: Yes, but with evidence. Like, “We observed 83 distinct prefix buckets for route=/assist/chat, top divergence occurs within first 120 tokens; estimated savings if normalized is X ms.” That’s the MVP.

[07:19] Ben Ward: How do you know where it diverges if you don’t have prompts?

[07:22] Logan Wright: We can log “matched_prefix_tokens” as a number. No content. Just how many tokens matched before diverging. Then you can chart distribution. If most partial hits match only 30 tokens, your stable prefix is tiny.

[07:37] Jin Park: That would be super useful. We don’t have that today.

[07:41] Omar El-Sayed: Right, and then saved_prefill_ms correlates with matched tokens, but it’s also hardware and model dependent. So we estimate based on observed prefill throughput in that window. It’s not perfect but it’s directionally correct.

[07:57] Maya Thompson: This is where we get skeptical. We’ve had vendors give “savings” numbers that don’t match.

[08:03] Omar El-Sayed: Totally fair. We usually validate saved_prefill_ms by comparing prefill latency distributions for cache hits vs misses in the same route/model cohort, controlling for prompt length. If the estimator says 40ms saved but you see no shift, something is wrong: classification, contention, or partial hits being counted as hits.

[08:22] Logan Wright: That’s why we separate hit-rate from hit-bytes and from saved_prefill_ms. One number is always misleading.

[08:30] Renee Sullivan: Jin, can you describe how your routing works? Because fragmentation is often the “invisible killer.”

[08:38] Jin Park: We do weighted routing across two model variants. And we do canaries on new versions, so a subset of traffic goes to version B. Sometimes we also route EU users to EU, US to US. For enterprise, some customers are pinned to a dedicated pool. So effectively, the same prompt could go to different “places.”

[08:57] Logan Wright: Yep, that’s fragmentation across model_version, region, and capacity tier. The recommendation could be: “pin route to a single model_version during peak hours,” or “align canary policy with cache warm-up,” or “don’t do 10% canary on all tenants if you care about caching.”

[09:16] Ben Ward: But we can’t just stop canaries.

[09:18] Aditya Rao: Not stop, but do it consciously. For example, canary on a smaller route first. Or canary on tenants where caching isn’t critical. Or accept that your hit-rate will drop during the rollout. Optimize can surface that as “expected drop due to rollout fragmentation.”

[09:35] Maya Thompson: That’s interesting. We do see hit-rate dips whenever we deploy and we weren’t sure if that was normal.

[09:43] Omar El-Sayed: It is normal unless your cache is shared across versions, which we don’t recommend because correctness and memory layout can change.

[09:50] Jin Park: On the telemetry fields—what do you need from the gateway vs runtime?

[09:56] Logan Wright: Runtime knows cache events: lookup, insert, evict, hit length. Gateway/control plane knows attribution: route_id, model_id, model_version, region, tenant_id, deployment_mode, and optionally “rollout_id” or “policy_id.”

[10:14] Logan Wright: The critical thing is consistent correlation so the cache outcome is attributed to the same request that billing and latency metrics use. Otherwise you get double counting and weirdness.

[10:26] Maya Thompson: Yep. We’ve had issues where our metrics pipeline counts retries as new requests.

[10:31] Omar El-Sayed: If you don’t have a stable request correlation ID across gateway and runtime, it’s very hard. But again: we don’t want to tag every metric with request_id. We want it in sampled debug events only.

[10:45] Jin Park: So for a pilot, what would you deploy? Like do you already have this?

[10:50] Renee Sullivan: We have a bunch of it. We’re in the middle of a “telemetry v2” cleanup, but for a Dedicated pilot we can enable the cache telemetry feature flag and give you dashboards. The improvements we’re doing are mostly around consistent definitions and better attribution tags, plus the “partial” classification.

[11:08] Aditya Rao: And for Optimize recommendations, MVP can work with aggregate counters plus a small sample of per-request events. The sample is mostly to generate “evidence links,” like example cohorts, not the actual prompts.

[11:22] Ben Ward: Evidence links meaning?

[11:24] Aditya Rao: In Console you click a recommendation and it shows: affected routes, time window, charts (hit-rate trend, prefix bucket count, matched_prefix_tokens distribution), and “what changed” signals like model_version mix shift.

[11:41] Maya Thompson: That’s exactly what we want: root cause-y.

[11:44] Jin Park: Okay, let’s talk metrics definitions. Our vendor says hit-rate is hits / (hits+misses). But what about partial?

[11:53] Logan Wright: We define three things typically:
- request_hit_rate = full_hits / cache_eligible_requests
- request_partial_rate = partial_hits / cache_eligible_requests
- byte_hit_rate = hit_bytes / eligible_bytes

[12:11] Logan Wright: If you collapse partial into hit, your hit-rate looks high but savings are low. If you collapse partial into miss, your hit-rate looks low but you may still be getting meaningful savings. So we keep them separate.

[12:24] Omar El-Sayed: For classification, a “full hit” might mean matched_prefix_tokens >= prompt_prefix_tokens - epsilon. Partial means > 0 but less than that. And “miss” is 0. There’s nuances with tokenizer boundaries and chunking.

[12:40] Alina Kovacs: Sorry, what is “prompt_prefix_tokens”? Like the whole prompt?

[12:45] Omar El-Sayed: Not the whole prompt. It’s the part that’s eligible to be cached. Usually system + maybe tool schema + some history, depending on your caching policy. Some people exclude recent chat turns because it changes a lot.

[12:59] Alina Kovacs: That’s helpful. We probably need to re-think what we consider “cacheable.”

[13:05] Aditya Rao: That becomes an Optimize rec: “Your cacheable prompt ratio is only 0.22; consider expanding eligibility window” or the opposite if you’re caching junk.

[13:16] Maya Thompson: Wait, opposite?

[13:18] Aditya Rao: Yeah. If you declare everything cacheable but your prefixes are super diverse, you waste memory and evict useful entries. Better to cache only stable prefixes.

[13:31] Jin Park: We’ve hit that. Memory pressure on GPU gets ugly.

[13:35] Omar El-Sayed: Exactly. Evictions can spike during traffic bursts and then your hit-rate collapses. So eviction metrics matter too: evict_count, evict_reason (capacity vs TTL), and cache_resident_bytes.

[13:50] Logan Wright: We usually keep evict_reason low cardinality: “capacity,” “ttl,” “manual,” “other.”

[13:57] Maya Thompson: If eviction is the cause, would you recommend bigger cache?

[14:01] Aditya Rao: Sometimes, but more often it’s: reduce prefix diversity, align routing, or change cache policy. Bigger cache is expensive.

[14:11] Ben Ward: We care about cost per answer, so yeah, not excited about just “buy more GPUs.”

[14:17] Renee Sullivan: This is where we can be really concrete in a pilot. We can compute “saved_prefill_ms” and also “tokens/sec improvement” and map to cost impact. Not perfect, but directional.

[14:32] Jin Park: Okay. What would success look like for you? Like, what numbers would prove value?

[14:38] Aditya Rao: For Optimize, we typically want to show: (1) we can measure cache effectiveness accurately and explain deltas, and (2) we can provide 3–5 actionable recs that lead to measurable improvement within a couple weeks. That could be +10 points byte_hit_rate, or -20ms p95 TTFT on cacheable routes, or reduced eviction spikes.

[15:00] Maya Thompson: Our main KPI is p95 TTFT for the assistant route. Also error rate during spikes.

[15:06] Omar El-Sayed: Cache helps TTFT more than decode. But if your bottleneck is decode, you might not see TTFT gains. That’s another reason telemetry should separate prefill vs decode latency.

[15:18] Jin Park: We can provide prefill/decode splits.

[15:21] Logan Wright: Great. If you can, also provide distribution of prompt lengths for that route, because caching benefits scale with prompt length.

[15:31] Alina Kovacs: We have a long tail. Some prompts are like 4k tokens with tools.

[15:36] Omar El-Sayed: Those are prime candidates—if you can normalize. But if every tool schema is customer-specific, it might never hit. Then you’re better caching just the system prompt segment.

[15:50] Ben Ward: We do per-customer tool defs, yeah.

[15:53] Aditya Rao: Then one suggestion is to separate “global tools” from “customer tools” and keep the global ones in a stable prefix. Or compress the tool schema.

[16:05] Alina Kovacs: That’s a big change but doable.

[16:09] Renee Sullivan: I want to check on data/privacy constraints. Maya, are there restrictions on telemetry leaving your environment?

[16:17] Maya Thompson: Yes. We can’t send raw prompts. We also can’t send per-request IDs that can be joined back to user identity. Aggregates are okay. Hashed buckets might be okay if it’s non-reversible and we control the salt.

[16:32] Logan Wright: That’s consistent with what we do. For the prefix buckets, we can let you choose: (a) compute bucket locally with your salt, or (b) don’t emit buckets at all and we rely on matched_prefix_tokens distribution. For the MVP, either works, but buckets make the “diversity” detector stronger.

[16:51] Jin Park: If we can compute locally, that’s best.

[16:55] Omar El-Sayed: Just note that if you change the salt daily, the bucket time series becomes useless.

[17:01] Maya Thompson: We can keep it stable per environment.

[17:04] Ben Ward: I want to understand how recommendations look. Are we talking emails? Dashboard cards?

[17:10] Aditya Rao: In the Console it’s a feed: each recommendation has title, impact estimate, evidence, and suggested action. For MVP we’re not doing fancy UI. But you can export as JSON too.

[17:24] Jin Park: We’d want API access.

[17:26] Aditya Rao: Yep, planned.

[17:29] Renee Sullivan: Let’s get specific: top three issues you think you have. My guess: prompt instability, routing fragmentation, and partial hits miscounted as full hits. Sound right?

[17:40] Jin Park: Yes. Plus we have multi-region and canaries.

[17:44] Maya Thompson: And also we need alerts. We can’t just look at dashboards. If hit-rate drops 20% after a deploy, we want a page or at least a Slack.

[17:54] Logan Wright: We do regression alerts using burn-rate style thresholds rather than absolute numbers, because traffic mix can change. Like: compare last 30 minutes vs last 6 hours baseline per route/model cohort, and only alert if the drop is sustained and the sample size is enough.

[18:12] Maya Thompson: That’s good. We’ve had noisy alerts when a customer with weird prompts spikes.

[18:18] Omar El-Sayed: Another pitfall: if you alert on request_hit_rate only, partial can mask issues. Better to alert on byte_hit_rate or saved_prefill_ms.

[18:28] Maya Thompson: saved_prefill_ms as an alert signal is interesting.

[18:31] Ben Ward: If it’s estimated, would you alert on it?

[18:34] Logan Wright: We’d alert on changes rather than absolute. And we’d pair it with a data-quality check: if estimator confidence is low, we don’t page.

[18:46] Jin Park: Okay. Switching gears: how does Dedicated deployment affect caching? We have customers that require data isolation.

[18:55] Renee Sullivan: Dedicated gives you isolated GPU pools, so caches are isolated by design, which is good for security. The tradeoff is smaller pools can have less reuse and more cold starts if traffic is bursty. So you’ll want to think about whether to share caches across tenants within the same Dedicated pool. Usually yes, but you can scope by tenant if required.

[19:15] Jin Park: Some tenants will require separation.

[19:18] Logan Wright: That’s why tenant attribution in telemetry matters. If you scope cache per tenant, you want to see the hit-rate per tenant and also the “overhead” of that isolation.

[19:30] Alina Kovacs: For prefix normalization, do you have examples or docs?

[19:35] Renee Sullivan: We have internal docs and some external guidance. I can share a checklist: stable system prompt, deterministic serialization, tool schema canonicalization, avoid per-request timestamps in the prefix, etc.

[19:49] Alina Kovacs: We literally include timestamps sometimes.

[19:52] Omar El-Sayed: Yeah, that kills caching instantly. Put timestamps after the cached prefix if you must.

[19:58] Ben Ward: We do it for “today’s date” reasoning.

[20:01] Aditya Rao: You can add date as a separate message later. Keep the top stable.

[20:07] Jin Park: This is good. Let’s talk about “partial-prefill” because that’s where we got burned. Our dashboards say 50% hit-rate but TTFT barely changes.

[20:18] Omar El-Sayed: Most likely those are partial hits being counted as hits. Or you’re hitting cache but still bottlenecked on something else, like CPU tokenization or queueing. Telemetry should include queue time too.

[20:31] Maya Thompson: We do have queue time spikes.

[20:34] Omar El-Sayed: If queue dominates, caching doesn’t help. But it still saves GPU time, which can reduce queue over time. It’s a second-order effect.

[20:45] Logan Wright: That’s why in dashboards we like “saved_prefill_ms” plus “concurrency” and “queue time.” It helps explain why savings didn’t translate to p95.

[20:57] Jin Park: Okay. So for a pilot, what do you need from us?

[21:03] Renee Sullivan: We need a representative route—maybe your assistant chat route—and a way to compare before/after. Ideally you run the same prompt templates with a synthetic workload too, so we can validate hit-rate measurement.

[21:18] Alina Kovacs: We can do synthetic. We have a replay harness.

[21:22] Omar El-Sayed: Great. Synthetic is perfect to validate “full hit vs partial” classification because you can craft exact repeats.

[21:31] Maya Thompson: And we need to see the dashboards.

[21:34] Renee Sullivan: Yep. I’ll share screenshots and also the panel list: global hit-rate, per-route breakdown, hit-bytes, saved-prefill-ms, cacheable prompt ratio, and drilldowns by deployment mode and region.

[21:50] Ben Ward: You said “cacheable prompt ratio.” How do you decide cacheable?

[21:54] Logan Wright: It’s based on policy and runtime constraints. For example: prompt length above threshold, cache enabled, not bypassed due to privacy mode, and request not using incompatible features. It’s basically: eligible_requests / total_requests. If it’s low, you’re not even in the game.

[22:13] Jin Park: We likely have bypasses for some tenants.

[22:16] Maya Thompson: Also, if you have sampling, does it break these ratios?

[22:21] Logan Wright: Aggregate counters are unsampled or use deterministic low-rate sampling with correction, depending on cost. For ratios used in alerts, we usually avoid heavy sampling. For per-request events, yes, sampled.

[22:36] Omar El-Sayed: The runtime path can’t afford to emit huge events for every token. We keep it lean: counters and occasional structured event.

[22:45] Alina Kovacs: How do you avoid overhead?

[22:48] Omar El-Sayed: We instrument at request boundaries and cache lookup/insert points, not per token. Also we do lock-free counters and batch export. And we put it behind a feature flag if anything goes sideways. Our target is less than 1% overhead at p95.

[23:06] Maya Thompson: If overhead is 1%, I’m okay. If it’s 10%, no.

[23:10] Omar El-Sayed: Same.

[23:12] Ben Ward: Can you talk about “prefix bucket” again. Is that actually safe?

[23:17] Logan Wright: It depends on implementation. If you hash the prefix and then modulo into 64 buckets, it’s not reversible. But it can still be sensitive if you use it wrong. We recommend: bucket count low, salt controlled by customer, and never log raw hash.

[23:34] Jin Park: That might pass our review.

[23:37] Renee Sullivan: We can also do “prefix diversity index” as a computed metric without buckets, but buckets are helpful for debugging and recommendations.

[23:49] Aditya Rao: For the MVP, the recommendation types we’re planning that would apply to you are:
1) Prompt prefix diversity high → normalize prompt templates
2) Routing fragmentation high → align/pin model/version/region for cacheable routes
3) Cache policy mismatch → adjust cache eligibility window or TTL
4) Rollout-induced regressions → change rollout strategy or expect drop

[24:10] Ben Ward: That’s basically it.

[24:12] Maya Thompson: Add “eviction storms” too.

[24:15] Aditya Rao: Yes, eviction-driven hit-rate collapses is on the list.

[24:21] Jin Park: Can you show an example of what you’d call “routing fragmentation high”?

[24:27] Logan Wright: Example: same route has traffic split across 4 model_versions in a 1-hour window, and each version has independent caches. Your effective cache size per version is smaller and warmup is repeated. We compute something like an entropy score over model_version distribution for cache-eligible requests. High entropy correlates with low byte_hit_rate.

[24:49] Jin Park: Got it. We have that during rollouts.

[24:52] Maya Thompson: Also during incidents when we fail over regions.

[24:56] Omar El-Sayed: Exactly. Failover is another fragmentation mode. Telemetry should include “fallback_reason” or “routed_via_fallback” boolean so you can separate “normal” from “degraded mode.”

[25:10] Maya Thompson: That would be huge. We often don’t know when routing changed.

[25:15] Renee Sullivan: We can incorporate that. Our routing attribution lead is Mina, but for pilots we can at least tag “policy_id.”

[25:24] Ben Ward: I’m going to ask about timeline. If we started a pilot, when can we actually get these dashboards?

[25:31] Renee Sullivan: For a Dedicated pilot, we can get you an initial set pretty quickly—within a week—assuming we can enable the telemetry flags and you’re okay with the data flow. The fancier recommendation feed is MVP and we can show early output but not perfect.

[25:47] Aditya Rao: We can start with manual analysis too: you send us metrics exports and we produce “recommendations” as a report. Then we automate.

[25:56] Jin Park: That might be acceptable.

[25:58] Alina Kovacs: I’d like to see the auto system eventually, but a report is fine to start.

[26:05] Maya Thompson: As long as we can validate.

[26:08] Logan Wright: Totally. We’ll also give you data-quality checks: missing tags, sampling misconfig, tag explosion symptoms.

[26:18] Jin Park: Tag explosion is my nightmare.

[26:21] Logan Wright: Same. That’s why we’re strict: route_id not route_name; model_id not arbitrary; version from a controlled set; region from a controlled set. If a tag value isn’t recognized, we drop or aggregate to “other.”

[26:39] Maya Thompson: That’s good but scary. If you drop, we might miss something.

[26:43] Logan Wright: We log “dropped_tag_events” as a metric, so you’ll see it. And we can sample raw events for debugging.

[26:53] Omar El-Sayed: Also, for runtime overhead, dropping tags early is cheaper than ingesting garbage.

[27:00] Alina Kovacs: Can we go back to “tool calling ordering.” We currently put tool definitions before system, sometimes.
